result.summary: Adonis ignores Venus's warning, hunts a boar and is gored to death. Venus, arriving too late, mourns him, promises a yearly rite of mourning, and turns his blood into a short-lived flower.

scenes.title: Adonis Hunts the Boar
scenes.summary: Venus leaves in her swan chariot, but Adonis keeps hunting. His dogs rouse a boar, he wounds it, and it kills him.
scenes.stakes: Adonis risks his life by chasing a wild boar against Venus's advice.

scenes.title: Venus Mourns and Makes a Flower
scenes.summary: Venus hears his groans, descends and laments. She sprinkles nectar on his blood, and a pomegranate-coloured flower springs up.
scenes.stakes: Venus faces the loss of her beloved and wants a lasting memorial.

alias_notes.explanation: A title of Venus, linked to the island of Cythera.

notable_quotes.reason: Venus founds the yearly commemoration of Adonis's death as a ritual of mourning.

analysis.text: Love and loss lead to transformation: grief becomes a lasting natural memorial. The fragile flower mirrors Adonis's brief life.
The passage links to the Adonia, an annual festival in which women mourned Adonis.

legacy.text: The myth of Venus and Adonis inspired Shakespeare's poem Venus and Adonis (1593) and many paintings, such as Titian's.

fun_facts.text: The flower is the anemone, whose Greek name relates to the wind (anemos), as sentence 12 alludes.

language_notes.text: Cytherea is a title of Venus, from the island of Cythera, near which she was said to have risen from the sea.
The yearly 'representation' of his death refers to the Adonia, a festival in which women mourned Adonis.
Refers to Proserpine (Persephone) turning the nymph Mentha into mint, told earlier in Ovid; Venus asks why she may not do likewise for Adonis.
The flower is the anemone, whose Greek name comes from anemos, 'wind'; the winds that name it also scatter its petals.

context_notes.text: Venus's swans draw her chariot; she had just warned Adonis to avoid dangerous beasts and hunt only timid game.
Adonis is called son of Cinyras, king of Cyprus, born of Myrrha's incestuous union with her father.

literary_notes.text: His courage resisting her advice signals that Adonis's disregard of the warning will bring disaster.
Venus addresses the dead Adonis directly, heightening her grief and her promise of lasting memorials.
The effervescing blood is compared to bubbles rising in rainy weather, giving the transformation a vivid, delicate image.
The flower's brief life, battered by wind, symbolizes the fragility of Adonis's beauty and of love and youth.
